hook.text: A sword tap on the shoulder makes a commoner a knight. One gesture changes your legal status.

buildup.text: Medieval knighthood required years of service as a page, then squire. The ceremony was the final exam.

discovery.text: The accolade—the actual dubbing—was often preceded by a full night of prayer and fasting.

twist.text: British knighthoods are now honorary. Sir Elton John and Sir Patrick Stewart share the same title as medieval warriors.

climax.text: Knighthood endures because people need visible markers of earned status. The sword is just a prop.

punchline.text: The sword changes nothing. The title changes everything.

quiz.question: What is the 'accolade' in the context of knighthood?
options: The act of dubbing with a sword

details.summary: Medieval knighthood was a rite of passage transforming a squire into a warrior of God through vigil, purification, and the dubbing ceremony. The knight knelt through a night of prayer, bathed for purification, and received a ritual sword-tap that conferred new identity and sacred obligations.
details.whyItMatters: Knighthood ceremonies demonstrate how medieval Europe used ritual to manufacture a warrior class bound by religious and social obligations. Modern honors systems descended from these rituals.
takeaways: Squires endured an all-night prayer vigil before knighting
The ritual bath symbolized spiritual purification
The dubbing — a blow or sword tap — formally conferred knighthood

faq.question: What was the process of becoming a knight?
faq.answer: A boy became a page at age 7, learning manners and basic combat. At 14, he became a squire, serving a knight directly. Around age 21, if deemed worthy, the knighting ceremony began with confession, fasting, an all-night prayer vigil (keeping vigil), ritual bathing, dressing in white, and finally.

faq.question: Are people still knighted today?
faq.answer: Yes, though the ceremony is now honorary rather than military. The British monarch knights people for service to society — a gentle sword tap on each shoulder at a formal investiture. Recipients become 'Sir' or 'Dame.' Other countries have equivalent honors.
